exercises.prompt: What is the type of `[1, 2, 3]` in OCaml?

options.label: `int list`, with three elements
options.feedback: Not yet. Commas build tuples; list elements are separated by semicolons.

options.label: `(int * int * int) list`, with one element
options.feedback: Yes. The commas build the triple `(1, 2, 3)`, and the brackets make a one-element list of it.

options.label: It is a syntax error.
options.feedback: Not yet. It is valid OCaml, which is what makes the mistake easy to miss.

hints: In OCaml, what does a comma build?
exercises.solution: The comma is the tuple constructor, so `1, 2, 3` is a triple, and `[1, 2, 3]` is a list containing that single triple: `(int * int * int) list`. The three-element list is written `[1; 2; 3]`.

```ocaml
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (List.fold_right (fun x acc -> x - acc) [ 10; 20; 30 ] 0)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. That is `((0 - 10) - 20) - 30`, a left fold. `fold_right` nests the other way.
Not yet. Work from the innermost parentheses: `10 - (20 - (30 - 0))`.

hints: `fold_right f [a; b; c] init` is `f a (f b (f c init))`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ocaml
let classify = function
  | [] -> "none"
  | [ x ] when x > 0 -> "one positive"
  | [ _ ] -> "one"
  | x :: _ :: _ when x mod 2 = 0 -> "many, even first"
  | _ -> "many"

let () =
  print_endline
    (String.concat " / " (List.map classify [ [ -3 ]; [ 4; 1 ]; [ 5 ]; [ 3; 3; 3 ] ]))
```
answers: one / many, even first / one positive / many

feedback.match: one positive / many, even first / one positive / many
feedback.message: Not yet. -3 fails the guard `x > 0`, so the next case, `[ _ ]`, matches.

hints: Try the cases from top to bottom for each list; a guard that fails sends you to the next case.
`x :: _ :: _` matches lists of at least two elements.
exercises.solution: `[-3]`: the guard `x > 0` fails, so `[ _ ]` gives `one`. `[4; 1]`: two elements, first even, so `many, even first`. `[5]`: `one positive`. `[3; 3; 3]`: the first element is odd, so the final `_` gives `many`. Joined: `one / many, even first / one positive / many`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ocaml
let () =
  let prices = [ ("tea", 3); ("coffee", 4) ] in
  let price item = Option.value ~default:(-1) (List.assoc_opt item prices) in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (price "coffee") (price "juice")
```
exercises.solution: `coffee` is in the list, so `List.assoc_opt` gives `Some 4` and `Option.value` unwraps it. `juice` is not, so the default, -1, is used. Output: `4 -1`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ocaml
let () =
  [ "3"; "three"; "30"; "0x10" ]
  |> List.filter_map int_of_string_opt
  |> List.fold_left ( + ) 0
  |> Printf.printf "%d\n"
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `int_of_string_opt` accepts the same syntax as OCaml integer literals, and `0x10` is hexadecimal for 16.

hints: OCaml integer literals can be written in hexadecimal with a `0x` prefix.
exercises.solution: `"three"` gives `None` and is dropped. `"3"` and `"30"` parse to 3 and 30, and `"0x10"` parses as hexadecimal 16, because `int_of_string_opt` accepts OCaml's literal syntax (including `0x`, `0o`, `0b` and underscores). 3 + 30 + 16 = 49. When parsing user input, check whether that flexibility is what you want.

exercises.prompt: Which operation takes constant time, whatever the length of the list `xs`?

options.label: `x :: xs`
options.feedback: Yes. It allocates one cell pointing at the existing `xs`, which is shared, not copied.

options.label: `xs @ [x]`
options.feedback: Not yet. Appending must copy every cell of `xs`.

options.label: `List.length xs`
options.feedback: Not yet. Lists do not store their length; `List.length` walks the whole list.

options.label: `List.nth xs 1000`
options.feedback: Not yet. Reaching element 1000 means following 1000 links.

hints: A list is a chain of cells, each pointing to the next.
exercises.solution: Only `x :: xs` is constant time: it creates a single new cell whose tail is the existing list. Appending, measuring and indexing all walk the list. When you need fast indexing, use an array (lesson 6).

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ocaml
let ( let* ) = Result.bind
let check n = if n > 100 then Error (Printf.sprintf "too big: %d" n) else Ok n

let () =
  let r =
    let* a = check 40 in
    let* b = check (a * 3) in
    let* c = check (b - 50) in
    Ok (a + c)
  in
  match r with
  | Ok v -> Printf.printf "ok %d\n" v
  | Error e -> print_endline e
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Check the second step: `a * 3` is 120, which is more than 100.

exercises.solution: `check 40` is `Ok 40`. `check 120` is `Error "too big: 120"`, and `Result.bind` passes an `Error` straight through without running the rest, so `r` is that error and the program prints `too big: 120`.
